messages.content: Write an internal post arguing for blameless postmortems at a company that does not do them yet. Around 250 words.

output:
**We should stop asking who broke it**

Last month's checkout outage got a writeup. It named an engineer in the second paragraph. Nobody said anything at the time, but I've watched what happened since: two people on that team now route every config change through a second reviewer they don't need, and the incident channel has gone quiet. That's the cost. We traded one honest account of a failure for a norm of not volunteering things.

Blameless postmortems aren't about being nice. They're a trade. We agree not to attach the failure to a person, and in exchange we get the actual sequence of events — including the part where someone had a bad feeling on Tuesday and didn't raise it, and the part where the runbook was three months stale and everyone knew.

You can't buy that information any other way. A person who expects to be named will give you a defensible narrative, and defensible narratives are useless for fixing systems.

The practical version is small. A facilitator who wasn't on call. A timeline written before anyone proposes fixes. Language rules in the doc: "the deploy script had no dry-run mode," not "Priya skipped the dry run." Action items with owners and dates, reviewed at the next one so they don't rot.

What this doesn't mean: no accountability. Someone who ignores a policy repeatedly is a management conversation, and a separate one. Conflating the two is why teams end up with neither.

I'll facilitate the next one if there's appetite. Reply here or grab me.
